scenes.text: In one experiment, people chose more pain over less pain, because of how it ended.
In nineteen ninety three, psychologists asked volunteers to hold a hand in painfully cold water.
In one trial, they held it in fourteen degree water for sixty seconds.
In the other, they did the same sixty seconds, then thirty seconds more.
But during those extra seconds, the water was warmed up by just one degree.
When asked which trial to repeat, most people picked the longer one.
It had more pain in total, but it ended a little better.
This is called the peak end rule, from Daniel Kahneman and Barbara Fredrickson.
We judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ends.
How long it lasted barely matters to the memory, which is called duration neglect.
In a later hospital study, some colonoscopies ended with a few extra calm minutes.
Those patients remembered the procedure as less unpleasant.
And they were more likely to come back for the next one.
Researchers still aren't completely sure why our memory works this way.
So if you want a good memory, give it a great ending.
What's an experience you remember mostly because of its ending?

title: Why people chose MORE pain in this experiment 🧊
caption: In a 1993 study, most people chose to repeat a longer cold-water trial because it ended slightly warmer. It's the peak-end rule: we remember the peak and the end.
